name: Avascular Necrosis

criteria.description: Presence of characteristic radiographic changes including sclerosis, subchondral radiolucency (crescent sign), and femoral head collapse
Localized joint pain exacerbated by weight-bearing and limited range of motion
MRI showing bone marrow edema, double-line sign, or focal necrotic lesions
Presence of known risk factors such as corticosteroid use, alcohol abuse, trauma, or coagulopathies

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical presentation plus radiographic or MRI evidence of bone necrosis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Early diagnosis often requires MRI as plain radiographs may be normal initially

pathognomonic.symptomName: Subchondral fracture with crescent sign on imaging
searchTerms: subchondral bone break with crescent sign

pathognomonic.symptomName: Localized deep joint pain aggravated by weight-bearing

common.symptomName: Reduced range of motion in affected joint
Joint stiffness especially after periods of inactivity
Limping gait when lower limb joints are involved
searchTerms: uneven walking due to joint pain

common.symptomName: Tenderness on palpation over affected joint

occasional.symptomName: Muscle atrophy adjacent to the affected joint

rare.symptomName: Systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever

searchTerms: joint shape changes due to wear

laboratory: Non-specific inflammatory markers usually normal or mildly elevated
Possible elevated serum lipid levels in some cases
Coagulation profile abnormalities in secondary causes
imaging: X-ray showing sclerosis, subchondral radiolucency (crescent sign), femoral head collapse
MRI demonstrating double-line sign, bone marrow edema, and necrotic lesions
Bone scan showing decreased uptake in early stages
genetic: Mutations associated with thrombophilia or hypofibrinolysis in some familial cases
other: Histopathology showing dead bone trabeculae with empty lacunae and surrounding reactive fibrosis

distinguishingFeatures: Gradual joint space narrowing without subchondral necrosis
Absence of crescent sign on imaging
More common in older adults with different pain pattern
Presence of systemic infection signs such as fever
Elevated inflammatory markers and positive joint fluid culture
Self-limiting condition with diffuse bone marrow edema on MRI

redFlags: Severe unremitting joint pain at rest or night
Signs of joint infection or systemic illness
references: Moya-Angeler J, et al. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head: pathophysiology and current concepts of treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2015;97(19):1620-1629.
Ficat RP. Idiopathic bone necrosis of the femoral head. Early diagnosis and treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1985;67(1):3-9.
